posts.title: Why Benchmarking AI/BI Genies Isn't Enough
posts.excerpt: Benchmark scores don't build trust in production AI. A well-defined semantic layer does.
posts.body:
Everyone loves AI benchmark scores. But in the real world, an AI tool being right 85% of the time doesn't cut it.



If an executive asks for quarterly revenue, they need a 100% accurate, unambiguous answer immediately. One bad number burns trust fast.



\## The Problem Isn't the Model



When tools like Databricks AI/BI Genie struggle, the reflex is to blame the LLM or tweak prompts. But raw model intelligence isn't the bottleneck.



The real fix happens before the AI generates an answer. It comes down to a well-defined semantic layer.



\## Data Engineering Over Model Hype



An AI agent is only as smart as the schema it sits on. A strong semantic layer gives the model hard guardrails:



\- Standardized business logic (defining "churn," "revenue," or "margin")

\- Clean table relationships to stop bad joins and double counting

\- Clear contextual metadata



The takeaway: benchmarks have their place, but solid data engineering is what makes conversational AI trustworthy.

posts.title: When "Average" Doesn't Mean What Data Engineers Think
posts.excerpt: Business users and data engineers often speak different languages. A simple metric like "average price" can silently break when real-world data pipelines fail.
posts.body:
A business user asks for a simple metric: "What's the average price over time?" 



To a data engineer, that sounds like a straightforward SQL query. But in production, the gap between what a user asks for and how a data pipeline behaves can lead to silent, expensive misinterpretations.



\## The Flaw in the Pipeline



I recently saw a real-world case of this. A team needed to track the rolling average price of a product. On paper, the logic was solid. But during a quiet system hiccup, the incoming live data feed was unexpectedly cut off.



Because the pipeline wasn't explicitly designed to handle missing time-series records, the calculation simply flat-lined—holding the last known prices steady instead of registering missing or zeroed inputs.



The result? The system output an "average" that was significantly higher than reality. 



\## The Dangerous Assumption



To the engine, the query was technically correct. To the user, it was completely misleading. 



If a decision-maker took that metric at face value, they would assume prices were holding strong when market activity had actually dropped off. They were imputing business stability from a silent pipeline failure.



\## Bridging the Context Gap



Data engineering isn't just about writing efficient transformation logic; it’s about understanding human context:



\- \*\*Expect explicit failure modes:\*\* If a feed drops, should the metric freeze, throw an alert, or gap out?

\- \*\*Validate business intent:\*\* Does the user want a strict mathematical average of available rows, or an accurate representation of time-bounded reality?

\- \*\*Build semantic context:\*\* Make pipeline health visible at the semantic layer so bad data never gets mistaken for a real business trend.



\*\*The takeaway:\*\* A query can be 100% syntactically correct and still be completely wrong for the business. True data quality happens where pipeline architecture meets real-world context.
